proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why does my salary feel fine until I actually look at my savings?"
description: "You earn enough. You spend carefully enough. But at the end of the month, the number in your savings account does not match the story you told yourself. Here is what is happening."
pubDate: 2026-07-07
tags: ["money avoidance", "money status", "behavioural finance"]
---

There is a version of this that most people who earn well will recognise.

The month starts fine. You are not reckless. You do not feel out of control. You have a vague, reasonable sense that the money is going to roughly the right places. Then, sometime around the 25th, you open your banking app and the number is smaller than it should be, and you close the app before you have to work out why.

Joel sees this in almost every client who comes to him earning above £60,000 a year. Not because they are bad with money. Because they have built a very effective system for staying just comfortable enough that a proper look never feels urgent.

The behavioural economics term for the mechanism is *present bias*: the discomfort of looking is immediate, and the cost of not looking is weeks away. So the brain trades a small future loss for immediate relief, every single time, until the pattern is years old.

The gym-bag version of this: Joel once found a gym bag under his bed that he had not opened in eight months. Inside it was an unopened tax-return envelope. He had £150,000 in deferred gains sitting in an account he had not logged into since the previous year. He is a qualified financial planner. The avoidance is not about knowledge.

That is the thing worth sitting with. The gap between what you earn and what you have built is rarely an information problem. It is a looking problem.

The question underneath is usually not "where did the money go?" It is "what would I have to face about myself if I actually tracked it?"

That is the work. Not the spreadsheet. Not the budget app. The quiet, honest reckoning with why the app keeps getting closed.
